reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Lemmel syndrome describes obstructive jaundice or biliary obstruction caused by a juxtapapillary (periampullary) duodenal diverticulum compressing or distorting the distal common bile duct, in the absence of choledocholithiasis or tumour

A periampullary diverticulum arises within a short distance of the major papilla, typically along the medial duodenal wall where mesenteric vessels and the biliopancreatic ducts penetrate the muscular layer, an area of relative wall weakness
Presentation overlaps with classic biliary obstruction: right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, jaundice, and deranged liver biochemistry, sometimes with recurrent cholangitis or pancreatitis

The diverticulum is frequently missed on ultrasound and may masquerade as a periampullary mass, a pancreatic cystic lesion, or a gas-containing collection on cross-sectional imaging if not specifically considered
Diagnosis is one of exclusion, requiring demonstration of a periampullary diverticulum together with biliary dilatation and no obstructing stone or neoplasm
Cross-sectional imaging and MRCP characterise the diverticulum and the biliary tree, while endoscopy directly visualises the diverticulum and its relationship to the papilla
Management is individualised: many patients are managed conservatively or endoscopically, while surgery (diverticulectomy or biliary bypass) is reserved for refractory or complicated disease
The syndrome is more common in older adults, in whom periampullary diverticula are increasingly prevalent, and it may complicate or coexist with gallstone disease
reference.pathophysiology: Periampullary duodenal diverticula are acquired outpouchings that herniate through a point of muscular weakness where vessels and the biliopancreatic ducts traverse the duodenal wall, becoming more frequent with advancing age as the wall loses elasticity. In Lemmel syndrome, such a diverticulum produces biliary obstruction through several overlapping mechanisms: direct mechanical compression of the intramural or distal common bile duct and papilla by a distended or food-filled diverticulum; distortion or angulation of the terminal bile duct and sphincter complex altering its anatomy and drainage; and chronic inflammation or fibrosis around the papilla (papillitis) impairing sphincter function and bile flow. Stasis within the diverticulum can also promote bactibilia and predispose to ascending cholangitis and to stone formation, while impaired pancreatic outflow may precipitate pancreatitis. The net effect is intermittent or progressive obstruction of bile drainage with proximal ductal dilatation and cholestasis, without an intrinsic ductal stone or tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Choledocholithiasis with distal common bile duct stone
Benign biliary stricture or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction
Chronic pancreatitis with distal duct stenosis
Mirizzi syndrome from an impacted cystic duct stone
additionalInvestigations: Liver biochemistry showing a cholestatic pattern with raised alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin
Abdominal ultrasound to assess biliary dilatation and exclude gallstones
Contrast-enhanced CT to characterise a periampullary diverticulum and exclude a mass
MRCP to delineate the biliary tree, the diverticulum, and the level of obstruction
Side-viewing endoscopy (duodenoscopy) to visualise the diverticulum and papilla directly
Endoscopic ultrasound to exclude a small periampullary or pancreatic tumour and assess the duct
ERCP where therapeutic intervention on the biliary tree is anticipated
redFlags: Features of acute cholangitis such as fever, rigors, jaundice, and haemodynamic instability
Progressive painless jaundice or weight loss raising concern for underlying malignancy
Signs of acute pancreatitis complicating the obstruction
Evidence of duodenal diverticular perforation such as peritonitis or retroperitoneal gas
Gastrointestinal haemorrhage from a bleeding diverticulum
reference.prognosis: With accurate diagnosis and appropriate endoscopic, medical, or surgical management the outlook is generally good, and many patients are controlled conservatively; prognosis worsens where complications such as recurrent cholangitis, pancreatitis, or diverticular perforation supervene, or where an underlying malignancy is initially overlooked.
pitfalls: Mistaking a gas- or debris-filled periampullary diverticulum for a pancreatic cystic lesion, abscess, or tumour on imaging
Attributing obstruction to the diverticulum without adequately excluding choledocholithiasis and periampullary malignancy
Overlooking a periampullary diverticulum on ultrasound and failing to pursue MRCP or endoscopy
Increased technical difficulty and higher complication risk of ERCP cannulation in the presence of a periampullary diverticulum
Failing to recognise the diverticulum as a source of recurrent cholangitis or pancreatitis in an older patient
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Blumgart's Surgery of the Liver, Biliary Tract and Pancreas
management: Relieve biliary obstruction endoscopically, using ERCP with sphincterotomy, biliary drainage or stenting as required
Treat associated acute cholangitis with appropriate antibiotics and urgent biliary decompression
Manage milder or intermittent obstruction conservatively with analgesia and monitoring
Reserve surgery such as diverticulectomy or biliary diversion for refractory obstruction or complications like diverticular perforation
Monitor liver biochemistry and watch for recurrent cholangitis or pancreatitis
Refer to hepatobiliary and endoscopy specialists for coordinated management
